# 1. Introduction

The digital transformation of education has become a major driving force in global educational reform, pro- foundly reshaping learning environments and teachers’ professional practice. In this process, teachers’ artiﬁ- cial intelligence (AI) literacy is not only a core vehicle for technology use but also a key prerequisite for the sustainable development of digital education (Le et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). The Artiﬁcial Intelligence Com- petency Framework for Teachers, released by the United Nations Educational, Scientiﬁc and Cultural Organ- ization (UNESCO) in 2024, explicitly identiﬁes AI literacy as a core competency for teachers in the era of intelligent education, encompassing technical proﬁciency, ethical re ection, and pedagogical innovation (UNESCO, 2024). In China, the Opinions on Accelerating the Advancement of Educational Digitalization and the Guidelines for General Artiﬁcial Intelligence Education in Primary and Secondary Schools, both issued in 2025, emphasize the importance of deep integration between AI and education for improving edu- cational quality. However, a substantial gap remains between policy aspirations and implementation in prac- tice. Relevant studies have shown that Chinese teachers still demonstrate limitations in both the breadth and depth of AI application in educational settings (Yang et al., 2023). Many teachers struggle to use AI tools proﬁciently to design inquiry-based learning activities, and most applications remain at the level of basic operation, lacking systematic pedagogical redesign and in-depth re ection on AI ethics (Chiu et al., [2024a)](#references). Although the National Smart Education Public Service Platform has registered more than 178 million users and aggregated over 130,000 high-quality resources for primary and secondary education,

This tension is closely associated with a “dual disconnect” in organizational support. First, at the resource level, there is a structural mismatch between supply and educational needs. Although schools have generally increased investment in intelligent hardware, the development of AI curricular resources, interdisciplinary case repositories, and technical support systems has lagged behind substantially (Zeng, 2022). This conﬁgur- ation pattern, characterized by an emphasis on hardware over content, places teachers in the dilemma of “having access to technology but being unable to use it e ectively,” thereby hindering the deep integration of AI into teaching. Second, at the mechanism level, school support tends to focus on short-term skills train- ing while neglecting the synergistic relationship between the cultivation of teachers’ innovation capability and their psychological readiness to accept technology. This fragmented support model fails to stimulate teachers’ intrinsic motivation and obstructs their transition from “technology users” to “educational innova- tors” (Xu & Zhu, 2023).

To address this dual disconnect, the present study draws on the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework (Tornatzky et al., 1990) and proposes a four-level collaborative framework consisting of insti- tutional support, resource coordination, mechanism innovation, and agent empowerment as a systematic sol- ution for narrowing the gap between policy aspirations and practical implementation. By progressively addressing the directional disconnect between macro-level policy and school-level implementation, the struc- tural mismatch inherent in the hardware-centered model, the fragmented support problem of short-term skills training, and teachers’ transformation from “technology users” to “educational innovators,” this framework 

1. ers an integrated and multilevel solution that connects organizational resource provision with individual capability development, providing a clear theoretical anchor for the subsequent empirical investigation.

In the international literature, teachers’ AI literacy has rapidly emerged as a growing area of research. Recent systematic reviews have shown that, although AI literacy is receiving increasing attention in K–12 education, research speciﬁcally focused on teachers’ AI literacy remains at an early stage (Biagini, [2025;](#references) Casal-Otero et al., [2023)](#references). Studies of preservice teachers further suggest that the development of AI literacy depends not only on external support such as training and curricular resources but also substantially on lear- ners’ motivation and attitudes (Lee & Song, 2024; Qian & Yan, 2026). By contrast, related research in the Chinese academic context has largely remained at the levels of information literacy and digital literacy, with relatively limited attention given to teachers’ AI literacy per se, especially to the role of organizational support mechanisms. Accordingly, this study raises a central question: How can school organizational support move beyond superﬁcial technological enablement and promote the deeper development of tea- chers’ AI literacy through the mediating roles of innovation capability and technology acceptance? Addres- sing this question can not only help bridge the gap between macro-level policy and micro-level practice but also provide actionable pathways for mechanism optimization and a systematic practical framework for advancing the digital transformation of education.

# 2. Literature review and research hypotheses

## _2.1. Theoretical framework: The Technology–Organization–Environment Model_

The Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework, proposed by Tornatzky et al. (1990), provides a systematic analytical perspective for understanding the process of technological innovation adoption at the organizational level. According to this framework, an organization’s decisions regarding technological innovation are jointly shaped by three key dimensions: the technological context, the organizational context, and the environmental context. The framework has been extensively validated in studies of infor- mation technology adoption and digital transformation (Baker, [2011;](#references) Gangwar et al., [2015)](#references) and, in recent years, has been widely applied to emerging technological domains such as blockchain adoption (Chittipaka et al., [2023)](#references) and artiﬁcial intelligence applications (Gupta et al., [2026)](#references). The TOE framework not only o ers a theoretical explanation for the mechanism through which organizational support operates, but also provides the theoretical foundation for understanding the chain transmission pathway of “organizational support → innovation capability → technology acceptance → AI literacy,” as shown in [Figure 1.](#22-applications-of-ai-in-education-and-other-sectors-implications-for-teachers-ai-literacy)

**Figure 1.** TOE Framework Application in Teachers’ AI Literacy Research.

The technological context encompasses the characteristics of technologies available both within and outside the organization, including attributes such as relative advantage, complexity, and compatibility. In the context of teachers’ AI literacy development, the technological context is re ected in technology accep- tance, particularly in terms of the functional features of AI tools, their operational complexity, and their com- patibility with existing instructional systems. These factors directly shape teachers’ perceptions of the usefulness and ease of use of AI technologies (Gangwar et al., [2015)](#references).

The organizational context re ects the internal characteristics and resource allocation of the organization, including management support, technological infrastructure, human resources, and organizational culture. In the present study, the organizational context is primarily re ected in school organizational support, encompassing dimensions such as work support, value recognition, beneﬁt-related care, interpersonal coordination, and professional development (Zhu et al., 2006). As the starting point of the chain mediation process, organizational support initiates the entire transmission mechanism by stimulating teachers’ tech- nology acceptance and innovation capability.

The environmental context encompasses the organization’s external institutional and competitive environment, including factors such as policies and regulations, industry standards, and competitive pressure, all of which are closely related to teachers’ innovation capability. In the development of teachers’ AI literacy, the environmental context is mainly re ected in policy orientations toward educational digitali- zation, development trends in the AI education industry, and society’s acceptance of AI in education. Among these factors, an innovative climate is particularly critical to teachers’ innovation capability (Ng et al., 2023).

The TOE framework aligns closely with the chain mediation logic of the present study and also provides theoretical support for the proposed four-level collaborative framework. Speciﬁcally, the three dimensions correspond to di erent stages of the chain transmission process: the organizational dimension initiates the chain, the technological dimension shapes the transformation process, and the environmental dimen- sion reinforces the transmission mechanism. Together, these dimensions constitute a comprehensive mech- anism underlying the development of teachers’ AI literacy. This multidimensional interactive mechanism provides a theoretical basis for understanding the pathways through which organizational support in u- ences teachers’ AI literacy.

## _2.2. Applications of AI in education and other sectors: implications for teachers’ AI literacy_

The widespread application of artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) across education and other sectors provides an important backdrop for understanding the signiﬁcance of teachers’ AI literacy. In education, AI technologies are demonstrating substantial transformative potential across multiple domains: personalized learning systems tailor content to individual students’ needs (Peng et al., 2019), intelligent tutoring systems 

| improve  | outcomes  | through real-time  | performance tracking  | (Ally  | & Perris,  | [2022)](#references),  | and  | adaptive  |  | assessment  |

| technologies  | o er  | continuous and  | dynamic feedback  | beyond  | the  | limitations  | of  | standardized  |  | testing  |
| (Chen et al.,  | [2020;](#references) |  Chiu, [2024;](#references) Du, [2025](#references) | [;](#references) Ng et al., 2023; |  Strielkowski et al.,  |  | 2025). |  |  |  |  |

AI is also reshaping curriculum development and content generation, with AI-driven tools enabling more responsive and learner-centered curricula (Abbasi et al., [2025)](#references) and generative AI assisting teachers in creat- ing diverse instructional resources (Long & Magerko, 2020). In assessment, automated scoring and feedback systems provide timely, scalable evaluation while generating formative data to inform instructional improve- ment (Qian & Yan, 2026). Learning analytics technologies support more precise instructional decision- making by mining educational data to reveal patterns in student learning behaviors (Tang et al., 2023). Fur- thermore, AI-integrated virtual learning environments are creating immersive and interactive spaces that extend the boundaries of conventional classroom instruction (Wang & Huang, 2025).

From a cross-sector perspective, successful AI applications in other ﬁelds also o er important insights for the development of AI in education and underscore the broader signiﬁcance of AI literacy. In healthcare, AI- driven diagnostic systems and clinical decision-support tools demonstrate how human expertise can be enhanced through human–AI collaboration, requiring professionals to develop the kind of AI literacy needed to work e ectively with intelligent systems rather than merely operate tools (Liaw et al., 2022; Topol, 2019; Zöller et al., 2025). In ﬁnance, algorithmic trading and risk assessment models illustrate that AI integration requires not only technical competence but also ethical awareness regarding algorithmic bias and decision transparency (Vuković et al., 2025; Yeo et al., 2025). In manufacturing, Industry 4.0 initiat- ives suggest that successful AI adoption depends on a comprehensive organizational support system, includ- ing systematic training, adaptive management structures, and an innovation-supportive culture (Ghobakhloo et al., [2022;](#references) Nayernia et al., 2022). Across these sectors, the evidence consistently indicates that AI literacy has become a foundational competency in contemporary society that transcends sectoral boundaries, and that its development depends critically on the organizational ecosystem rather than on indi- vidual e ort alone (Casal-Otero et al., [2023)](#references).

These cross-sector insights suggest that the development of teachers’ AI literacy must be understood within the broader context of professional transformation, in which learning technologies are reshaping the fundamental nature of teaching practice (Strielkowski et al., 2025). E ective AI literacy development requires simultaneous attention to technological understanding, evaluative skills, practical application, and ethical considerations (Ng et al., 2023; Pinski & Benlian, 2024), while the rapid iteration of AI technologies demands continuous professional learning (Su et al., 2023).

This context highlights the critical role of organizational support in the development of teachers’ AI lit- eracy. In response to the growing di usion of AI technologies and the urgent demands of educational digital transformation, school organizations must provide systematic support to ensure that teachers are able to respond e ectively to the educational challenges of the intelligent age.

## _2.3. Research hypotheses_

#### _2.3.1. The e_ _ect of organizational support on teachers’ AI literacy_

Perceived organizational support (POS), deﬁned as individuals’ overall perception that the organization values their contributions and cares about their well-being, is re ected in educational settings through the resource support, value recognition, beneﬁt-related care, and professional empowerment that schools provide to teachers (Rhoades & Eisenberger, 2002). Prior research has shown that high levels of organiz- ational support can foster a positive instructional ecology by providing explicit resources, such as technical training and equipment provision, as well as implicit support, such as cultivating a culture that encourages innovation, thereby strengthening teachers’ conﬁdence in using intelligent technologies to improve instruc- tion (Shen et al., 2024). Particularly in the context of rapid AI development, organizational support provides teachers with the necessary conditions and motivational backing to access, learn, and apply AI tools. Accord- ing to the TOE framework, when teachers strongly perceive organizational support, they are more likely to engage in activities that enhance their competence, strive to meet organizational expectations, and realize their self-worth (Chiu et al., [2024b)](#references). Empirical studies further indicate that perceived organizational support serves as a key mediating mechanism through which leadership behaviors are translated into positive pro- fessional outcomes (Sluss et al., 2008). Teachers with stronger perceptions of organizational support are 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 5

more likely to proactively acquire new knowledge and to experiment with integrating technology into class- room practice, thereby gradually enhancing their AI literacy through practice (Futris et al., [2015)](#references). Accord- ingly, this study proposes the following hypothesis: 

H1: Organizational support has a signiﬁcant positive e ect on teachers’ AI literacy.

### _2.3.2. The mediating role of innovation capability_

Innovation capability refers to teachers’ core ability to identify problems, generate creative ideas, and implement novel solutions in instructional practice, encompassing innovative thinking, practical transform- ation, and adaptability (Lin & Liu, 2025; Qin et al., 2025). Organizational support can e ectively stimulate tea- chers’ creative exploratory behavior by providing professional development resources, such as interdisciplinary collaboration platforms and technological experimentation spaces, as well as innovation- oriented incentive mechanisms, such as incorporating AI application into performance evaluation (Zargar et al., 2025). Research has shown that, in educational contexts shaped by the rapid development of AI, tea- chers with stronger innovation capability are more likely to move beyond traditional instructional frame- works and proactively explore innovative applications of AI in education (Chen et al., [2020)](#references). For example, they may use intelligent learning analytics tools to design personalized learning pathways or employ gen- erative AI to create interactive instructional content. This innovation-oriented process of practice not only deepens teachers’ understanding of the functions and potential of AI technologies but also promotes the comprehensive development of their AI literacy through an iterative cycle of technological exploration, ped- agogical innovation, and re ective improvement (Tang et al., 2023).

Furthermore, teachers with stronger innovation capability demonstrate greater adaptability in response to evolving AI technologies, enabling them to integrate tools creatively into instructional design (Dilek et al., [2025;](#references) Mazman Akar, 2019; Scherer et al., 2019). Innovation capability thus serves as a critical bridge linking organizational support and AI literacy by transforming external resources into teachers’ intrinsic motivation to learn and apply AI technologies. Accordingly, this study proposes the following hypothesis: 

H2: Innovation capability mediates the relationship between organizational support and teachers’ AI literacy.

### _2.3.3. The mediating role of technology acceptance_

Technology acceptance refers to teachers’ psychological level of acceptance of AI technologies and is driven by perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use (Venkatesh & Davis, 2000). Recent research has shown that teachers’ digital literacy can signiﬁcantly in uence their willingness to use AI-based instructional tools through pathways such as perceived usefulness, behavioral attitudes, and subjective norms (Du, [2025)](#references). Organizational support enhances teachers’ recognition of the educational value of new technologies, such as precise learning analytics and personalized feedback, through systematic training, while also lower- ing barriers to use by simplifying technological procedures. Research further indicates that the widespread application of AI has brought transformative changes to education, from personalized learning to intelligent assessment, all of which require teachers to possess an adequate level of technology acceptance (Chen et al., [2020)](#references).

Teachers with higher levels of technology acceptance are more likely to embed AI tools into instructional design and assessment, thereby accumulating practical experience and developing a more sophisticated understanding of AI technologies (Casal-Otero et al., [2023;](#references) Dilek et al., [2025)](#references).

Moreover, teachers’ technology acceptance directly a ects the e ectiveness of their AI-supported instruc- tional practices and their capacity for continuous improvement (Long & Magerko, 2020; Tang et al., 2023). Therefore, technology acceptance may serve as a key psychological pathway through which organizational support is translated into AI literacy. Accordingly, this study proposes the following hypothesis: 

H3: Technology acceptance mediates the relationship between organizational support and teachers’ AI literacy.

#### _2.3.4. The chain mediating e_ _ects of innovation capability and technology acceptance_

The mechanism through which organizational support in uences AI literacy is not a simple linear relation- ship; rather, it involves a spiral process driven by the synergistic e ects of innovation capability and 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Figure 2.** The Eﬀect Model of Perceived Organizational Support on AI Literacy.

technology acceptance. Organizational support empowers teachers’ innovation capability by providing resources and incentive mechanisms (Hammond et al., [2009)](#references), while enhanced innovation capability further promotes deeper understanding and acceptance of AI technologies, facilitating teachers’ transition from “passive learning” to “active innovation” (Chen et al., [2020)](#references), as shown in [Figure 2.](#3-method) This chain pathway of “innovation-driven technological internalization” enables multidimensional alignment among resource allo- cation, capacity building, and psychological acceptance, re ecting the developmental trajectory from basic tool use to deep integration that characterizes AI adoption in education (Dilek et al., [2025;](#references) Tang et al., 2023).

As a multidimensional competency framework, AI literacy requires teachers not only to master technical operational skills but also to develop critical thinking and innovative application capabilities (Long & Magerko, 2020; Zhou et al., 2025). Therefore, the chain mediating e ects of innovation capability and tech- nology acceptance provide an important theoretical perspective for understanding how organizational support systematically promotes the development of teachers’ AI literacy. Accordingly, this study proposes the following hypothesis: 

H4: Innovation capability and technology acceptance exert a chain mediating e ect on the relationship between organizational support and teachers’ AI literacy.

# 3. Method

## _3.1. Data source_

The research team conducted a large-scale survey of primary and secondary school teachers across all 16 districts of Shanghai to systematically examine the current status of teachers’ organizational support, AI lit- eracy, and related factors. A total of 11,581 questionnaires were collected through the Wenjuanxing plat- form. After a rigorous quality-control procedure, including the removal of questionnaires containing logical inconsistencies, excessive missing data, and highly repetitive response patterns, 10,683 valid responses were retained, yielding an e ective response rate of 92.25%.

The survey employed a stratiﬁed random sampling method. First, the 16 districts of Shanghai were divided into three tiers according to their level of economic development: central urban districts (Huangpu, Jing’an, Xuhui, and Changning; four districts), inner suburban districts (including Minhang, Baoshan, Jiading, and Pudong; eight districts), and outer suburban districts (Jinshan, Chongming, Feng- xian, and Qingpu; four districts), thereby ensuring that the sample covered areas with di erent levels of development. Within each district, a second stage of stratiﬁcation was conducted by school type (public vs. private) and educational level (primary school, junior secondary school, and senior secondary school), after which teachers were randomly selected from each school to participate in the survey. To ensure data quality, the research team established strict quality-control criteria, including a minimum completion time of 8 min, logical consistency checks across related items, and outlier screen- ing, with questionnaires excluded when the proportion of consecutively selecting the same option was excessively high.

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 7

The sample exhibited multidimensional heterogeneity. In terms of gender, 3,519 respondents were male (32.94%) and 7,164 were female (67.06%). With respect to educational level, the sample was well distributed across primary schools (21.83%, n = 2,332), junior secondary schools (50.83%, n = 5,430), and senior second- ary schools (27.34%, n = 2,921). Regarding educational background, 184 teachers (1.72%) held an associate degree or below, the majority held a bachelor’s degree (71.36%, n = 7,623), and 26.92% held a master’s or doctoral degree (master’s: n = 2,784; doctoral: n = 92). Anonymity was strictly maintained throughout the data collection process.

## _3.2. Variable selection_

### _3.2.1. Organizational support_

This study adopted the classic Perceived Organizational Support (POS) scale developed by Eisenberger et al. ([1986)](#references), drawing on its revised version for the Chinese organizational context and adapting the wording of the items to re ect the professional characteristics of teachers. Speciﬁcally, the adaptation involved four steps. First, linguistic localization was conducted through a translation–back-translation procedure, in which two doctoral students in education independently translated the items and cross-checked the results to ensure semantic accuracy. Second, contextualization was implemented by replacing generic organizational expressions in the original scale with education-speciﬁc terminology; for example, “organiz- ation” was uniformly changed to “school,” and “job performance” was revised to “teaching performance.” Third, item screening was carried out to remove statements irrelevant to the teaching profession while retaining 15 core items in light of the work characteristics of Chinese teachers. Fourth, some items were cul- turally reﬁned; for instance, “management” was replaced with “school leadership” to better align with the cultural context of Chinese education. These adaptations were necessary because the original scale devel- oped by Eisenberger et al. ([1986)](#references) was designed for general organizational settings and did not fully capture the distinctive features of organizational support for teachers in schools, including instructional lea- dership, the provision of teaching resources, and support from professional learning communities. A pilot test involving 120 teachers from two schools in Shanghai conﬁrmed that the adapted items demonstrated better face validity and comprehensibility than a direct translation of the original version.

The scale consisted of 15 items (A1–A15) covering ﬁve dimensions: work support, value recognition, beneﬁt-related care, interpersonal coordination, and professional development. All items were measured on a ﬁve-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 5 (“strongly agree”), with higher total scores indicating stronger perceived organizational support. All items were positively keyed. Reliability and validity tests showed that the Cronbach’s α coe cients for the ﬁve dimensions were 0.949, 0.962, 0.965, 0.970, and 0.957, respectively. The conﬁrmatory factor analysis showed a good model ﬁt (GFI = 0.932, RMSEA = 0.079, CFI = 0.977, NFI = 0.976), indicating strong internal consistency and structural validity.

### _3.2.2. Teachers’ AI literacy_ Given the dynamic evolution of the concept of literacy in the digital era – from information literacy to digital literacy and, more recently, AI literacy – this study integrated the AI literacy scale developed by Nong et al. (2024) with the Artiﬁcial Intelligence Competency Framework for Teachers proposed by the United Nations Educational, Scientiﬁc and Cultural Organization (UNESCO, 2024) to construct a localized AI literacy scale. The adaptation process involved four steps. First, the theoretical framework was localized by adjusting the com- petency structure in light of the policy requirements set forth in China’s Teachers’ Digital Literacy Standards and the AI Plus Teacher Workforce Development Action Plan. Second, item content was revised by convert- ing technology-development-oriented statements in the original scale into teaching-application-oriented items; for example, “being able to program AI algorithms” was revised to “being able to select appropriate AI tools to support instruction.” Third, cultural contextualization was undertaken by simplifying certain tech- nical terms and adding pedagogically situated descriptions in consideration of Chinese teachers’ levels of understanding of AI technologies. Fourth, expert review was conducted by inviting ﬁve experts in AI edu- cation and 10 frontline teachers to evaluate the content validity of the scale, after which ﬁnal revisions were made based on their feedback. These adaptations were necessary because the original scale developed by Nong et al. (2024) was intended primarily to assess general AI literacy across di erent groups and did not speciﬁcally address teachers’ instructional application contexts or the policy requirements of Chinese education. Integration with the UNESCO framework ensured international alignment, whereas the localiz- ation process responded to the practical reality that Chinese primary and secondary school teachers typically use AI as an instructional tool rather than as a technology development platform. A pilot study with 80 tea- chers conﬁrmed that the revised items accurately captured the intended dimensions of AI literacy in the Chinese K–12 teaching context.

The scale included 18 items (B1–B18) across six dimensions: AI thinking, AI ethics, AI foundations, AI peda- gogy, AI tools, and teachers’ professional learning, all measured on a ﬁve-point Likert scale. Reliability analy- sis showed that the Cronbach’s α coe cients for the six dimensions were 0.900, 0.952, 0.927, 0.940, 0.953, and 0.893, respectively. The conﬁrmatory factor analysis met acceptable standards (CFI = 0.931, NFI = 0.930, NNFI = 0.912, IFI = 0.931), conﬁrming the sound psychometric properties of the scale.

### _3.2.3. Innovation capability_

The innovation capability scale was adapted from the teacher innovation capability scale proposed by Sharma and Sharma (2018) to re ect the characteristics of teachers’ instructional practice. The revision process involved four steps. First, translation and cultural adaptation were conducted through a standard procedure of forward translation, back translation, and expert review to ensure the accuracy and compre- hensibility of the items in the Chinese context. Second, educational contextualization was implemented by revising generic innovation-related statements in the original scale into pedagogically oriented expressions; for example, “I often look for new ways of working” was changed to “I often explore new teach- ing methods.” Third, item reduction was undertaken to balance questionnaire length and teacher response burden, resulting in the selection of 9 representative items from the original 12-item scale. Fourth, linguistic localization was applied to make the wording more natural and uent in accordance with Chinese teachers’ expression habits. These revisions were necessary because the original scale was designed for general organ- izational settings and did not fully capture the distinctive features of instructional innovation in K–12 edu- cation. The reduction from 12 to 9 items was guided by item – total correlations and factor loadings from an exploratory factor analysis based on a pilot sample of 150 participants, as well as substantive judgments regarding relevance to the Chinese teaching context.

The scale comprised 9 items (C1–C9) across three dimensions: innovative thinking (e.g. “I often think about how to make teaching more creative”), innovative practice (e.g. “I try to use new technologies to support teaching”), and innovative disposition (e.g. “I value continuous learning and improvement”). All items were measured on a ﬁve-point Likert scale. Reliability testing showed that the Cronbach’s α coe cients for the three dimensions were 0.975, 0.947, and 0.975, respectively. The conﬁrmatory factor analysis yielded excellent ﬁt indices (GFI = 0.946, RMR = 0.018, CFI = 0.983, NFI = 0.983), providing strong support for the reliability and validity of the scale.

### _3.2.4. Technology acceptance_

This study used the technology acceptance scale developed by Davis ([1989)](#references) as the basis for the question- naire and adapted it for Chinese teachers. The modiﬁcation process involved four steps. First, the target tech- nology was speciﬁed by replacing all generic references to “information technology” in the original scale with “AI technology” to ensure consistency in the measurement focus. Second, educational contextualization was introduced by embedding teaching scenarios into the items; for example, “this technology is useful” was revised to “AI technology can improve teaching e ciency.” Third, item optimization and selection were con- ducted by choosing 6 core items from the original 12-item scale in order to streamline the questionnaire and sharpen its focus. Fourth, linguistic localization was applied by adopting wording consistent with the expression habits of Chinese teachers to ensure naturalness and comprehensibility. These modiﬁcations were necessary because the original scale targeted general information technology systems in workplace settings, whereas AI technology acceptance in educational contexts involves distinct considerations such as pedagogical appropriateness and alignment with curricular goals. A pilot study with 80 teachers conﬁrmed that the shortened scale retained a stable two-factor structure with strong factor loadings (all \> 0.70).

The scale consisted of two dimensions: perceived usefulness (e.g. “AI technology can improve teaching e ciency”) and perceived ease of use (e.g. “AI tools are simple and convenient to operate”). It included 6 items (D1–D6), all measured on a ﬁve-point Likert scale, with higher total scores indicating a stronger 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 9

tendency toward technology acceptance. Data analysis showed that the Cronbach’s α coe cients for the two dimensions were 0.952 and 0.963, respectively. The conﬁrmatory factor analysis produced strong model ﬁt indices (GFI = 0.969, RMR = 0.016, CFI = 0.988, NFI = 0.987), indicating that the scale e ectively cap- tured teachers’ psychological acceptance of AI technologies.

## _3.3. Data analysis_

This study used SPSS 26.0 and Amos 26.0 for data analysis. SPSS 26.0 was used for data preprocessing, includ- ing reliability analysis (Cronbach’s α), descriptive statistics, and Pearson correlation analysis. Amos 26.0 was used for conﬁrmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modeling (SEM) with maximum likelihood (ML) estimation to examine the direct and mediating pathways. The bias-corrected percentile Bootstrap method with 5,000 resamples was employed to test mediating e ects, with a 95% conﬁdence interval (CI) not including zero taken as evidence of signiﬁcance. Model ﬁt was evaluated using indices including CFI, NFI, and RMSEA.

# 4. Results

## _4.1. Common method bias_

To control for the potential in uence of common method bias on the study ﬁndings, Harman’s single-factor test was applied to the measurement items for organizational support, innovation capability, technology acceptance, and AI literacy. The results showed that ﬁve latent factors with eigenvalues greater than 1 were extracted, and the ﬁrst factor accounted for 37.3% of the total variance, which is below the critical threshold of 40%. This result indicates that the data were not substantially a ected by common method bias and that the ﬁndings are therefore credible.

## _4.2. Descriptive statistics and correlation analysis_

The overall mean score for teachers’ AI literacy was 3.656 (SD = 0.827). Signiﬁcant di erences were observed across the subdimensions. AI ethics (M = 4.091) and AI thinking (M = 3.881) showed the highest levels of per- formance. Teachers’ professional learning (M = 3.543) and AI tools (M = 3.513) were at a moderate level. By contrast, AI pedagogy (M = 3.497) and AI foundations (M = 3.409) were relatively weak, suggesting that tech- nological application capability and the integration of pedagogy remain the most salient shortcomings, as shown in [Table 1.](#33-data-analysis)

These ﬁndings reveal a structural imbalance in the development of teachers’ AI literacy and carry impor- tant theoretical implications. The relatively weak performance in AI foundations (M = 3.409) suggests that teachers have an insu cient understanding of the principles and functions of AI technologies, which directly constrains their ability to use AI tools exibly in instructional practice and may result in a pattern of appli- cation characterized by procedural use without deeper conceptual understanding. This ﬁnding is consistent with the technological context dimension of the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework, which posits that technological complexity signiﬁcantly a ects adoption outcomes (Tornatzky et al., 1990). Without su cient foundational knowledge, teachers cannot e ectively evaluate the suitability and limit- ations of di erent AI tools in speciﬁc instructional contexts, causing their technology acceptance to remain at the level of superﬁcial compliance rather than deep integration.

The relatively lagging performance in AI pedagogy (M = 3.497) further indicates that teachers have not yet developed the capacity to integrate AI technologies organically with pedagogical approaches, which may lead to surface-level and fragmented applications of technology. This gap in pedagogical integration re ects the environmental context dimension of the TOE framework, speciﬁcally the lack of innovation-sup- portive mechanisms that would enable teachers to experiment with AI-enhanced instructional design in authentic teaching contexts (Kundu & Roy, [2023)](#references). These two weaknesses reinforce each other. Limited AI foundational knowledge constrains teachers’ ability to envision innovative pedagogical applications, whereas weak AI pedagogy reduces opportunities to deepen foundational understanding through practice. Together, they constitute a major bottleneck in the improvement of teachers’ AI literacy.

The chain mediation framework proposed in this study – organizational support → innovation capability → technology acceptance → AI literacy – provides a systematic pathway for addressing this structural imbal- ance. Through the four-level collaborative framework, organizational support can strengthen AI foundational knowledge via training platforms, stimulate innovation capability through collaborative research and inter- disciplinary experiments, and gradually enhance technology acceptance, thereby promoting the coordi- nated development of both AI foundational and pedagogical competence. This chain mediation mechanism thus links the empirical ﬁndings to a practical intervention framework.

The correlation analysis among the variables ([Table 2)](#43-testing-of-the-chain-mediation-model) showed that organizational support was signiﬁ- cantly and positively correlated with innovation capability (_r_ = 0.636, _p_ \< 0.001), technology acceptance (_r_ = 0.558, _p_ \< 0.001), and AI literacy (_r_ = 0.605, _p_ \< 0.001). Innovation capability was also highly correlated with technology acceptance (_r_ = 0.677, _p_ \< 0.001) and AI literacy (_r_ = 0.720, _p_ \< 0.001). The correlation coe - cient between technology acceptance and AI literacy reached 0.850 (_p_ \< 0.001), indicating a strong synergis- tic relationship among these three factors.

## _4.3. Testing of the chain mediation model_

Based on the research hypotheses, this study constructed a structural equation model with organizational support as the independent variable, teachers’ AI literacy as the dependent variable, and innovation capa- bility and technology acceptance as the chain mediators, in order to systematically examine the mechanism linking these variables. The model ﬁt indices were as follows: CFI = 0.896, NFI = 0.896, RMR = 0.063, SRMR = 0.088, PGFI = 0.547, PNFI = 0.732, and PCFI = 0.732. Although the CFI and NFI values were slightly below the conventional threshold of 0.90, these indices are known to be sensitive to model complexity under large- sample conditions (N = 10,683) and may therefore underestimate model ﬁt to some extent (Cheung & Rensvold, [2002)](#references). Both the RMR and SRMR were below the criterion of 0.10, and the parsimony-adjusted ﬁt indices (PGFI, PNFI, and PCFI) all exceeded 0.50, indicating that the model achieved an acceptable ﬁt while maintaining parsimony. Taken together, the overall model ﬁt was acceptable.

The path analysis results ([Figure 3)](#5-discussion-and-conclusion) showed the following standardized path coe cients. First, organiz- ational support signiﬁcantly and positively predicted innovation capability (β = 0.666, _p_ \< 0.001), technology acceptance (β = 0.192, _p_ \< 0.001), and AI literacy (β = 0.043, _p_ \< 0.001), conﬁrming its signiﬁcant predictive role. Second, innovation capability exerted cross-level transmission e ects on both technology acceptance (β = 0.605, _p_ \< 0.001) and AI literacy (β = 0.029, _p_ \< 0.01). Third, the standardized path coe cient from tech- nology acceptance to AI literacy reached 0.870 (_p_ \< 0.001), highlighting its reinforcing role as the core mech- anism of transformation. These ﬁndings support the theoretical proposition that organizational support 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 11

**Figure 3.** Path Analysis Results of the Chain Mediation Model.

enhances teachers’ AI literacy through a pathway characterized by innovation-driven development and tech- nological internalization.

To test the robustness of the mediating e ects, this study applied the bias-corrected percentile Bootstrap method with 5,000 resamples to examine the path relationships ([Table 2)](#43-testing-of-the-chain-mediation-model). The results reported below are unstandardized e ect estimates. The ﬁndings showed that: (1) the direct e ect of organizational support on AI literacy was 0.110 (95% CI = \[0.097, 0.122\]), accounting for 18.2% of the total e ect, thereby supporting H1; (2) the indirect e ect of innovation capability in the pathway from organizational support to AI literacy was 0.136 (95% CI = \[0.124, 0.148\]), accounting for 22.4% of the total e ect, thereby supporting H2; (3) the indirect e ect of technology acceptance was 0.138 (95% CI = \[0.122, 0.154\]), accounting for 22.8% of the total e ect, thereby supporting H3; and (4) the chain mediating e ect of innovation capability and technology acceptance reached 0.222 (95% CI = \[0.210, 0.235\]), accounting for 36.6% of the total e ect, thereby support- ing H4. These results indicate that organizational support not only directly empowers teachers’ AI literacy but also promotes it through a chain mechanism of innovation capability development followed by the psycho- logical internalization of technology. Together, these pathways accounted for 81.8% of the total e ect, high- lighting the central logic of the three-dimensional mechanism linking resources, capability, and psychological processes.

# 5. Discussion and conclusion

Based on the structural equation modeling analysis, this study elucidates the pathways and underlying mechanisms through which organizational support enhances teachers’ AI literacy. Drawing on empirical data from 10,683 teachers in Shanghai, the study conﬁrms four key ﬁndings and further clariﬁes their deeper implications for the digital transformation of education.

### _5.1. Core ﬁndings: the multifaceted mechanism of organizational support_

The ﬁndings show that organizational support has a signiﬁcant direct e ect on teachers’ AI literacy (0.110, _p_ \< 0.001), accounting for 18.2% of the total e ect. This indicates that the provision of resources, value recognition, and professional development support by schools can directly enhance teachers’ ability and willingness to apply AI technologies (Moreira et al., 2019). Through both tangible support, such as technical training and hardware provision, and intangible support, such as fostering an innovative climate, organiz- ational support e ectively shortens the transition from “technological awareness” to “instructional appli- cation” (Xie et al., 2023), consistent with the core proposition of the TOE framework.

Innovation capability also plays a signiﬁcant mediating role in the relationship between organizational support and AI literacy, with an indirect e ect of 0.136, accounting for 22.4% of the total e ect. By providing professional platforms, incentive mechanisms, and spaces for innovation, organizational support e ectively cultivates teachers’ innovative thinking and practical capability, thereby promoting their integration of AI technologies into instructional design (Lin, 2021). This pathway underscores the central importance of capacity building in technology use, suggesting that merely having access to technological tools is not su cient; teachers must also develop the capability to use these tools for pedagogical innovation (Hulpia et al., [2011)](#references).

Technology acceptance likewise serves a signiﬁcant mediating function (indirect e ect: 0.138, 22.8% of total e ect), as organizational support enhances teachers’ perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use (Scherer et al., 2021). Most importantly, innovation capability and technology acceptance jointly constitute the strongest chain mediation pathway (e ect: 0.222, 36.6% of total e ect), forming a progressive pathway of “innovation-driven development → technological internalization” (Chen et al., [2020;](#references) Dilek et al., [2025;](#references) Hammond et al., [2009;](#references) Tang et al., 2023). This ﬁnding highlights the critical value of the synergy between external support and teachers’ endogenous factors in technology adoption.

## _5.2. The four-level collaborative framework and the mechanism for advancing the digital transformation of education_

Based on the empirical ﬁndings, this study proposes a four-level collaborative framework – comprising insti- tutional support, resource coordination, mechanism innovation, and agent empowerment – as a practice- oriented support system for advancing the comprehensive digital transformation of education (see [Figure 4)](#6-theoretical-and-practical-implications).

This framework moves beyond a narrow focus on individual teachers’ competency development and pos- itions organizational support as a systemic lever for institutional change. The level of institutional support provides the policy environment and normative foundation for the intelligent development of the education system, including the establishment of AI education standards, the formulation of technology integration policies, and the creation of accountability mechanisms that align institutional incentives with the goals of digital transformation (Chiu, [2024;](#references) Dilek et al., [2025;](#references) Ng et al., 2023).

The level of resource coordination provides material and soft-resource support for the intelligent trans- formation of the education system by prioritizing the development of curricular resources, technical support infrastructure, and professional learning communities, thereby addressing the documented imbal- ance of emphasizing hardware while neglecting content (Abbasi et al., [2025;](#references) Shen et al., 2024). The level of mechanism innovation stimulates stakeholders’ intrinsic motivation to participate in digital transformation by establishing incentive and evaluation systems that reward pedagogical innovation and by creating col- laborative governance mechanisms that promote knowledge sharing across schools and disciplines (Lin & Liu, 2025; Qin et al., 2025). The level of agent empowerment systematically enhances teachers’ AI literacy through the chain mechanism of “innovation capability → technology acceptance,” while also fostering stu- dents’ digital competence and improving the digital adaptability and innovative capacity of all participants in the educational system (Scherer et al., 2019; Zhang & Zhang, 2024).

Importantly, this framework aligns with emerging global discourse on the digital transformation of edu- cation, which emphasizes that sustainable technology integration requires simultaneous change at the policy, institutional, pedagogical, and individual levels rather than fragmented interventions (Strielkowski et al., 2025). The four-level collaborative framework advances educational digital transformation through three core mechanisms. First, the vertical penetration mechanism ensures the e ective transmission and implementation of policy intentions (Shen et al., 2024). Second, the horizontal coordination mechanism creates a uniﬁed force for digital transformation (Qin et al., 2025). Third, the spiral enhancement mechanism enables cyclical feedback and iterative optimization, thereby forming a spiral trajectory for the digital trans- formation of education (Strielkowski et al., 2025).

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Figure 4.** Four-Level Collaborative Framework for Advancing Educational Digital Transformation.

This framework drives the digital transformation of education as a multilayered process that extends beyond the improvement of teachers’ AI literacy alone. At the micro level, the chain mediation pathway enables a shift from traditional knowledge transmission to intelligent and personalized teaching (Scherer et al., 2019; Zhang & Zhang, 2024). At the meso level, the framework promotes data-driven educational man- agement, as organizations that support innovation capability simultaneously build institutional capacity for evidence-based governance (Eryilmaz et al., [2025;](#references) Shen et al., 2024). At the macro level, the framework facili- tates the formation of a digital education ecosystem in which government, schools, the technology industry, and teachers converge toward shared transformation goals (Abbasi et al., [2025;](#references) Saeedikiya et al., 2025; Strielkowski et al., 2025). By embedding technological change within comprehensive reforms involving insti- tutions, resources, mechanisms, and human agency, this framework achieves an integration of technology- driven change with the intrinsic logic of educational development (Dilek et al., [2025;](#references) Lin & Liu, 2025; Ng et al., 2023). The ﬁnding that the chain mediation pathway accounts for 36.6% of the total e ect provides quan- titative support for the argument that digital transformation requires coordinated organizational, cognitive, and psychological mechanisms rather than isolated technological provision.

In conclusion, this study reveals the full mechanism through which organizational support enhances tea- chers’ AI literacy via direct e ects (18.2%) and indirect e ects (81.8%), and constructs a four-level collabora- tive framework that enables an organic linkage between the enhancement of teachers’ literacy at the micro level and the transformation of the education system at the macro level through vertical penetration, hori- zontal coordination, and spiral enhancement mechanisms.

# 6. Theoretical and practical implications

## _6.1. Theoretical implications_

This study contributes to the theoretical literature on the development of teachers’ AI literacy in three major ways. First, it extends research on the antecedents of teachers’ AI literacy. Existing studies have focused pri- marily on teachers’ individual characteristics while paying insu cient attention to organizational environ- mental factors. By incorporating organizational support into the analytical framework, this study veriﬁes its role as a key external driving force, ﬁlls a theoretical gap concerning the in uence of macro-level organ- izational factors on teachers’ AI literacy, and enriches the application of the Technology–Organization– Environment framework in the ﬁeld of education.

Second, this study reveals the mediating mechanisms through which organizational support in uences teachers’ AI literacy. By introducing innovation capability and technology acceptance as mediating variables, the study not only conﬁrms their respective independent mediating e ects but also identiﬁes, for the ﬁrst time, the chain mediating e ect of “innovation capability → technology acceptance.” This ﬁnding establishes a theoretical model in which organizational factors promote teachers’ technological literacy through a pathway of “capacity building → psychological acceptance,” thereby o ering a new perspective for under- standing the interactive mechanism between organizational environments and teachers’ individual characteristics.

Third, this study develops an integrated theoretical framework for the development of teachers’ AI lit- eracy. Speciﬁcally, it advances a multilayered developmental model of “organizational resources → teacher capability → psychological acceptance → literacy performance,” providing teacher education theory with a new perspective on the coordinated development of external support and internal motivation. This theoretical framework helps move beyond the binary divide between “individual-centered” and “organ- ization-centered” approaches in teacher development research and contributes to a more integrated theory of teachers’ professional development.

## _6.2. Practical implications_

At the practical level, this study o ers three speciﬁc recommendations for education administrators, school leaders, and policymakers. First, the ﬁndings underscore the critical role of organizational support in foster- ing teachers’ AI literacy. Accordingly, education administrators are advised to move beyond a narrow focus on hardware provision and instead build a comprehensive support system that encompasses technological resources, professional training, incentive mechanisms, and an innovation-supportive culture.

Second, the mediating e ects of innovation capability and technology acceptance account for 22.4% and 22.8% of the total e ect, respectively, indicating the critical role of teachers’ endogenous factors in translat- ing organizational support into literacy outcomes. Schools should therefore establish a dual-track teacher development system. On the one hand, they should cultivate teachers’ innovation capability through project-based learning and interdisciplinary collaboration. On the other hand, they should enhance teachers’ technology acceptance through demonstration lessons and the sharing of successful cases. Given that the chain mediating e ect of “innovation capability → technology acceptance” accounts for 36.6% of the total e ect, schools should give priority to fostering innovation capability.

Third, this study provides a practical framework for building a multi-stakeholder system to support the development of teachers’ AI literacy. Based on the four-level structure of institutional support, resource coordination, mechanism innovation, and agent empowerment, government agencies need to strengthen policy guidance and resource investment; schools need to optimize their internal incentive and support mechanisms; and teachers need to enhance their innovative awareness and self-directed learning capacity. Such a multilayered support system can generate synergistic e ects and provide a systematic solution for the sustainable development of teachers’ AI literacy.

# 7. Limitations and future research

This study has four main limitations, each of which points to directions for future research. First, the study adopted a cross-sectional design and therefore can capture only correlational relationships among variables rather than establish causality. Future studies could employ experimental or longitudinal designs to track changes in teachers’ AI literacy by intervening in levels of organizational support, thereby providing a more rigorous test of causal relationships.

Second, this study relied exclusively on questionnaire data, which may raise concerns regarding common method bias. Although this risk was addressed through Harman’s single-factor test, with the ﬁrst factor accounting for 37.3% of the variance, below the 40% threshold, future research should nevertheless consider 

INTERACTIVE LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS 15

mixed-methods approaches. Integrating classroom observation, in-depth interviews, and case analysis could yield richer multidimensional data and enhance both the reliability and explanatory power of the ﬁndings.

Third, although the sample size was relatively large (N = 10,683), the participants were limited to teachers in Shanghai, which may restrict regional representativeness. Given regional disparities across China in edu- cational resources, levels of informatization, and support for teachers’ professional development, future research should expand the sampling frame to include teachers from central and western regions as well as rural areas. Comparative analyses across regions would help clarify how di erent organizational support mechanisms in uence teachers’ AI literacy and would strengthen the external validity of the ﬁndings.

Finally, this study did not take into account potential moderating variables such as teachers’ individual levels of technological competence and disciplinary backgrounds. Future research could examine the mod- erating roles of individual di erences, such as technological proﬁciency and subject characteristics, as well as structural factors, such as policy environments and resource investment, in the pathways through which organizational support in uences teachers’ AI literacy. This would enable the development of a more com- prehensive theoretical model. In addition, given the rapid evolution of AI technologies, future studies could incorporate related variables such as digital literacy and computational thinking into the analytical frame- work in order to explore the broader mechanisms underlying the development of teachers’ digital competence.

In sum, future research should further advance the theoretical and practical study of teachers’ AI literacy development by expanding regional coverage, enriching research methods, reﬁning variable systems, and deepening comparative analysis, thereby providing more scientiﬁc and systematic support for the digital transformation of education.
